AIRO

You just got here: using AIRO to inherit a project

Foundational 50 minutes Lab 2 of 2
Introduction

In this lab, you'll act as IT Admin for Cardboard Brands, inheriting a project and using AIRO to explain, debug, and fix it before Alex Kim, a new Sales hire, starts Wednesday.

SC
Sam Chen
IT Admin · Cardboard Brands

Inherited a Project with no handover notes, and a new Sales hire starting Wednesday.

The question

With no documentation, no original builder, and no human solution architect to ask, how much of that missing expertise can AIRO actually stand in for?

You'll learn how to

  • Get a high-level orientation of the Project given to you, then trace one recipe's logic in detail
  • Fix two bugs in the prebuilt recipes by describing symptoms to AIRO, not guessing at causes

What you'll need

  • Access to the training project (recipes ONB-001 through ONB-005)
  • Access to Playgrounds, to see the Kanban boards
  • About 50 minutes, uninterrupted
Phase 1

Get your bearings

In this phase, you'll get a high-level orientation of the Project given to you, then trace one recipe's logic in detail.

Pattern

Solution-architect stand-in

AIRO has read every recipe in this project and can explain how they connect, the way the original builder would have — if they'd left notes. Ask it the way you'd ask a colleague who inherited the project before you.

1.1

Figure out what you've inherited

Sam Chen's manager asks how the project assigned to you works. The person who built it left the company with no handover notes, and Sam Chen has never opened it. Before touching anything, they need the big picture.

Overview

Open the project you've inherited (WOW-XXX[AIRO]) and ask AIRO what it does, at a level a colleague could explain in thirty seconds: what the recipes are, and how they connect. AIRO has read every recipe already; you haven't opened any of them yet.

Detailed steps 3 steps

This task is orientation only: no build, no fix. It sets up Task 1.2, where you trace one specific recipe's logic in the same way.

  • From wherever Lab 1 left you, go back to the Projects section and open the project given to you.
  • Open AIRO and ask: What does this project do? AIRO has already read every recipe and determined where it sits in the workspace, inside your project; one question replaces what would otherwise be an hour of clicking through each recipe by hand.
  • Ask the follow-up: Give me a high-level summary and explain how the recipes and connectors connect. A list of recipe names isn't an explanation; asking for how they connect is what tests whether AIRO understands the trigger-to-action chain.
Verify AIRO's summary names the project's recipes and describes at least one real trigger-to-action chain, not only a list of recipe names.
1.2

Go deeper into one recipe

Sam Chen's manager asks them to walk through the onboarding recipe on a call in ten minutes. They've never opened it.

Overview

Ask AIRO to identify the main orchestrator recipe, then have it walk you through that recipe's logic in plain language. Push it with an edge case before you trust your own summary.

Detailed steps 5 steps

Task 1.1 gave you the project shape. This task tests whether AIRO's explanation of one recipe holds up against a real question you didn't script, an edge case, not only a happy path.

  • Ask AIRO: Identify the main orchestrator recipe in this project. AIRO already understands how the recipes are architected, so it can point you to the right one instead of you tracing every connection yourself.
  • Open the main recipe mentioned by AIRO and ask: Walk me through this recipe, adding comments step by step. When AIRO offers to add the comments, click to accept, then click Apply updates to commit them to the recipe. Comments left in the recipe become a permanent trace of AIRO's explanation, useful even after this session ends.
    HintIf you closed AIRO's chat to do this, click Chat history next to New chat and pick up the conversation you were just in for Task 1.2.1. Starting a new chat here would lose the context AIRO already built in this task.
  • Ask a follow-up: What happens if a required field is missing? Note whether AIRO points to an existing guardrail or flags a real gap. A happy-path summary and a summary that survives an edge case aren't the same thing; this is the edge case that tells them apart.
  • Now that you understand the recipes, start all of the recipes so the automation runs and syncs over the IT and HR tickets. If you're unsure how to start a recipe, ask AIRO. Then go visit Playgrounds to see the tickets synced over for IT and HR. If you don't know how to get there, revisit Lab 0 – Visit Playgrounds.
  • Without successful jobs running, Playgrounds' Kanban board and job report won't have anything real to check against. Check your job report or Playgrounds to confirm the records actually synced.
Verify you can state the recipe's trigger, its main steps, and at least one edge case, without having opened the recipe yourself first.
Phase 2

Debug what's broken

In this phase, you'll fix two bugs in the prebuilt recipes by describing symptoms to AIRO, not guessing at causes.

Pattern

Symptom-first debugging

A solution architect doesn't need you to diagnose the bug before you talk to them; they need the symptom. Describe what's wrong; the error message, the incorrect output; rather than guessing at a cause yourself. AIRO localizes the fault faster from a clear symptom than from a hunch.

2.1

Fix the wrong data type

IT asset tickets for new hires are showing a due date of 1999-01-01. The recipe runs without erroring at the trigger, but syncs incorrectly. Nobody who built the recipes is around to ask.

Overview

If you haven't done Visit Playgrounds yet, go there first and explore the HR and IT boards, that's where the actual symptom is sitting, not only in a recipe's job report. Then describe the symptom to AIRO exactly as you'd describe it to a solution architect on call: what's wrong, not what you think caused it. Get AIRO's explanation before you apply anything, then confirm the fix against a real job.

Detailed steps 7 steps

This is the first of two recipe bugs. The pattern here (symptom first, explanation before fix, verify against a real run) is the one you'll repeat in Task 2.2 on a harder bug.

  • If you haven't already, open Playgrounds. Use an IT Admin persona (for example, Sam Chen) to look at the IT tickets, then go to the IT Support board — you can open any IT Asset Request ticket under To do and look at its due date. Does it seem right? Seeing the symptom on the real board, not only hearing it described, gives you something concrete to check AIRO's answer against.
  • Ask AIRO: The due date on new IT asset tickets is showing 1999-01-01. What's wrong? None of the recipes throw an error or show up in any failure log, so there's nothing to search for; AIRO finds the bug by reading the recipe's logic directly, the same way a solution architect would open the recipe instead of grepping for an exception.
  • Before applying anything, make sure you understand the root cause: the correct due date should be 7 days from today, formatted YYYY-MM-DD. Applying a fix you can't explain relocates the mystery instead of closing it.
  • Follow up with: Does anything else look off with the due date in other recipes? A hardcoded value that's wrong once is often copied everywhere else it was used.
  • If AIRO offers more than one way to fix it, the correct one computes the due date as 7 days from today, formatted YYYY-MM-DD, not the hardcoded 1999-01-01. Apply the fix, and compare the field before and after. Note which value it replaced and why the original failed. Comparing before and after confirms the fix matches AIRO's explanation, not only that something on the screen changed.
    HintIf AIRO asks you to stop all recipes before applying the fix, follow its instructions before continuing — recipes can't be safely edited while they're actively running, so stopping first avoids the fix landing mid-job. If a pop-up warns that unsaved changes will be lost, click OK; that warning is triggered by stopping the recipe itself, not by any manual edit you made, so it's expected even if you haven't touched anything yourself.
  • Repeat the same record in the job history. The job history shows the ticket key and ticket summary, so you can match what you see there to the Playgrounds IT board. If you're unsure how to repeat a job, ask AIRO to walk you through it step by step.
  • Revisit Playgrounds and check the IT Support Kanban board to confirm the change is actually reflected there, not only in the job report. A job report says the recipe ran; the board is what actually changed.
Verify the due date step now computes 7 days from today, formatted YYYY-MM-DD, instead of the hardcoded 1999-01-01 string, and the recipe test-runs without a parsing error.
2.2

Fix the broken conditional logic

In the same IT ticketing from Task 2.1, look at the IT Asset Request tickets. Each person should receive the right IT assets: Sales should receive Sales equipment, and everyone else should receive HR equipment.

Overview

This bug doesn't announce itself the way a runtime error does. Describe the symptom to AIRO, but work out the root cause yourself before AIRO tells you, then confirm your answer against its explanation. If a Sales rep escalates a wrong equipment order next quarter, you're the one explaining what happened and why it's fixed — not AIRO, so you need to actually understand the cause, not just repeat what it told you.

Apply these values

Sales Asset Provisioning

  1. Laptop: Dell Latitude 7440 (lightweight, travel-durable build)
  2. Mobile hotspot / mobile broadband card (for offsite client visits)
  3. Mobile device: iPhone SE / company phone plan
  4. Peripherals: Wireless keyboard + mouse, headset (no monitor, travel-first role)
  5. Laptop bag / travel case

HR Asset Provisioning

  1. Laptop: Dell Latitude 5440 (i5, 16GB RAM, 256GB SSD)
  2. Docking station (desk-based role)
  3. Monitor: Single 24" monitor
  4. Peripherals: Wireless keyboard + mouse, headset
  5. Access badge / key fob
Detailed steps 5 steps

Task 2.1 was a silent failure too — a bad hardcoded value. This one is a silent failure of a different kind: correct-looking output that's actually wrong, because the bug is in the architecture of the logic itself, the conditional branch, not a bad value. AIRO's role here is the same as a solution architect reviewing the implementation: it reads the actual conditional logic, not just the output, so it can catch a bug the output alone would never reveal.

  • In Playgrounds, open an IT Asset Request ticket for a non-Sales person (for example, Max Rue) on the IT Support board and check whether the correct equipment was provisioned.
  • Describe the symptom to AIRO: A non-Sales employee's IT Asset Request ticket shows the Sales equipment list instead of the HR one. No error was thrown. What's wrong?
  • Compare your answer to AIRO's, apply the fix, and confirm the logical condition now reads "Sales" in department instead of "Sales" not in department.
  • Make sure the logic is correct: confirm the fix actually applies to real, already-synced records, not only to new tickets going forward.
  • Once the recipe has been fixed, you can repeat the job for the records in Workato and check Playgrounds to see if they've been provisioned the correct assets.
Verify you can state the actual root cause, the flipped operator, in your own words before AIRO tells you. Confirm by checking ticket descriptions: Sales tickets should show the Sales Asset Provisioning list, and everyone else should show the HR Asset Provisioning list (see above).

Reflect

Now that Project is explained, traced, and two bugs into the fix, consider what you'd trust AIRO with next time.

  • Did AIRO's project summary in Task 1.1 match what you'd expect from opening the recipes yourself? What did it get right, and what did it miss?
  • Neither bug threw an error — one was a hardcoded value, the other a flipped condition buried in the logic. AIRO found both without a single stack trace to point it there. What does that tell you about the kind of failures AIRO can catch that a monitoring dashboard, which only watches for thrown errors, never would?
  • You were asked to state Task 2.2's root cause before reading AIRO's explanation. Did you actually do that, or did you skim ahead? What does the answer tell you about how you'll use AIRO going forward?

Wrap-up

Sam Chen started the day with a project they'd never opened and two bugs nobody had time to explain. By the end, they could describe all of it themselves, in their own words, not only repeat what AIRO told them.

  • AIRO reads the actual logic, not just the output. That's how it caught two bugs that never threw a single error — a hardcoded value and a flipped condition — either one could have run for months undetected without it.
  • Diagnose it yourself first, then compare notes with AIRO. If you only ever take its answer, you have no way to catch it when it's wrong — and a silent bug like these two won't announce itself to tell you AIRO missed something. That habit is what makes you faster over time, not AIRO alone.

Bonus challenges

These are optional, open-ended extensions. There aren't any more click-by-click instructions; reach for what you built.

  • Build the offboarding counterpart. Project is the employee onboarding project, it has no counterpart for employees leaving. IT has written up exactly what they want in a real PRD, a recipe and a Genie, each with its own trigger. Submit the PRD directly to AIRO and ask it to build both assets from it, in one go, rather than translating each requirement into your own prompt.

Grab the PRD from FileStorage: in Workato, go to Tools > FileStorage, and find PRD - Employee Offboarding.

Run it, then read the PRD to confirm what AIRO built actually covers the guardrails: the trigger condition, the duplicate guard, and the ticket fields it creates. One ticket should be processed for David Chris — check the result against the PRD. Then build the Genie's two skills, sending a manager notification on demand and reading ticket status, and try asking it to do something neither skill covers, updating or closing a ticket directly, to confirm it correctly refuses instead of improvising an action.

Verify both assets end-to-end: the recipe creates a correctly-fielded ticket without duplicating one that already exists, and the Genie only ever touches tickets by reading them, never by writing to them.
